newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - European bourses hold breath, await U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - European bourses hold breath, await U.S. data.

text.p: An overnight drop on Wall Street did little to shake European share markets on Friday but interest rate jitters ahead of important U.S. inflation figures dominated sentiment.
European bourses shrugged off the Dow Jones industrial average's 24-point overnight fall to move broadly higher at their opening.
But nervousness ahead of U.S. March retail sales and producer price figures, scheduled for release at 1230 GMT, put shares under pressure as investors took profits ahead of any potential surprises.
Investors will study the data for clues about the timing of the next interest rate rise.

"The U.S. figures are clearly of extreme importance to the market. If these figures are stronger than the market expects it will increase the likelihood of a near-term U.S. rate rise," said NatWest UK equities strategist David McBain.
A Reuters poll of economists forecast U.S. retail sales to rise 0.6 percent compared with February and producer prices to remain unchanged.
"We will probably anyway see one or two rate hikes there in the next few months taking U.S. rates up about 50 basis points," McBain said.
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised its key federal funds rate for the first time in nearly 14 months on March 25 with a 25 basis point increase.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar remained firm, although it was trapped in a tight range as dealers await the next signal on the dollar's direction from the inflation figures.
A robust U.S. economy and expectations of higher interest rates have been the main engine of the dollar's latest bull run.
Market sentiment on the dollar's strength against the yen had not changed noticeably following confusing comments from Japanese officials overnight about concern over the yen's recent slide.

Cabinet minister Kabun Muto cautioned that an artificial attempt to forestall a further slide by the yen might not be effective. But the Ministry of Finance quickly distanced itself from his comments saying they did not reflect official policy.
The ministry emphasised that the official view was that the yen's recent falls were overdone and the ministry was concerned about it.
Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International in London, said the dollar's run could also begin to eat into U.S. corporate earnings.
"If we don't get intervention from the central banks, the dollar is going to keep on rising, which has to have an impact on earnings," he said.
The dollar is currently trading near a three-year high against the German mark and 57-month high versus the yen.

Sterling proved the strong performer on European markets, climbing to 2.80 marks for the first time since September 1992, when it was ejected from the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM). The pound first topped its old ERM floor at 2.7780 marks on Monday.
The dollar's continued strength underpinned German shares for much of the session before slipping a little towards the end to be down 0.34 percent.
Investors see weakness of the once-mighty mark translating into higher profits for the country's big exporters.

German carmaker Volkswagen AG, whose shares on Thursday jumped through the important 1,000 mark ($581) barrier, surged nearly 10 percent in early Friday trade on the back of a positive business outlook for the 1997 year.
London shares made a strong opening showing, with the FTSE-100 index climbing 0.34 percent at the open before retreating slightly.
French shares were marginally lower at midsession.
CURRENCIES AT 1140 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.7225 marks and 126.07 yen, compared with 1.7177 and 126.02 in late European trade on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1140 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 5.7 points at 4,318.9.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 11.44 points at 3,340.05.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index was 0.23 points lower at 2,607.74.
PRECIOUS METALS AT 1140 GMT
Gold was fixed in the morning at $348.65 an ounce, compared with the London close of $347.85 on Thursday. Silver was one cent lower at $4.80.
